en: The Commentary on the Twenty Verses (Viṃśikāvṛtti):

This [world] is indeed representation-only (vijñaptimātra), because there is the appearance of non-existent objects, just like the vision of non-existent hair-nets and so forth by one suffering from ophthalmia. (Vvṛ 1)

If representation does not exist by way of an external object, then there would be no restriction of place and time, nor would there be a lack of restriction regarding mental continua, and the performance of purposeful action would not be possible.
The restriction of place and so forth is established as in the case of dreams;
furthermore, the lack of restriction regarding the mental continuum is seen by all in the perception of rivers of pus and the like.

The performance of functions is like [the effects] of a dream; furthermore, everything regarding the vision of hell-wardens and the like, as well as the suffering inflicted by them, is like [the experience of] hell.
The birth of animals occurs in heaven just as it does in hell;
however, this is not the case for hungry ghosts (pretas), because they do not experience the suffering born of those realms.
If it is thus accepted that the arising and transformation of the elements there occurs through those karmas, why is this not also accepted for consciousness?

The latent impression of an action is conceived as being in one place while its fruit is conceived elsewhere; why indeed is it not accepted to be in the very same place where the impression exists? Vvṛ 7.
The existence of the sense-bases such as form was spoken with a specific intention toward those people who were to be trained by him, just like [the teaching on] spontaneously born beings.
There is no sentient being here, nor a self; rather, these phenomena exist together with their causes.
From its own seed, a representation arises appearing as such-and-such;
the Sage spoke of those two as the twofold sense-bases for that [representation].
Thus, indeed, there is the entry into the selflessness of the person;
otherwise, however, there is the teaching for the entry into the selflessness of phenomena by way of the imagined nature.
That object is neither one nor many in terms of atoms;
nor are they [atoms] joined together, because the atom itself is not established.
Through simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts;
because the six occupy the same location, the entire mass would be no more than a single atom.
If there is no conjunction of atoms, then in their aggregate, whose conjunction could it be?
Nor is it established through their conjunction because of [the claim that] they lack parts. (Vvṛ 13)
For that which possesses a division into parts, unity is not tenable;
or else, how could there be shadow and obstruction? If it is not a composite whole, then those two do not belong to it.
If [the sense-faculty] were a single unity, there could be no sequential perception, nor simultaneous perception and non-perception;
furthermore, there would be no occurrence of multiple distinct functions, nor the non-perception of subtle objects.
Just as the cognition of direct perception occurs in dreams and the like, at that time the object is not seen; how, then, can its status as a direct perception be maintained?
It has been stated that representation appears as such [an object], and from that, memory arises;
one who has not awakened does not realize the non-existence of the objects perceived by a dreamer. (Vvṛ 17)
The restriction of representation occurs mutually through the state of being dominant over one another;
because the mind is impaired by torpor in a dream, the result is not the same [as in the waking state].

Death is a transformation resulting from a specific representation of another, just as the loss of memory and other such states occur in others through the power of the minds of beings such as piśācas.
Or how did the Daṇḍaka forest become empty through the anger of the sages? And how is it established by that [example] that the punishment of the mind is a great offense? Vvṛ 20.

How can the knowledge of those who know the minds of others be non-conformable to reality, given that it is like the knowledge of one's own mind, or like the object-domain of a Buddha, which is beyond [ordinary] cognition? // Vvṛ 21 //
This proof of representation-only has been composed by me according to my own capacity;
however, it is in every respect inconceivable, being the domain of the Buddhas.
The Twenty Verses on the Proof of Cognition-Only.
This is the work of the Master Vasubandhu.
